units.text: ⟦0⟧5.5 Character Classes and Bracket Expressions⟦1⟧
units.sourceHTML: 5.5 Character Classes and Bracket Expressions

units.text: A ⟦0⟧bracket expression⟦1⟧ is a list of characters enclosed by ‘⟦2⟧’ and ‘⟦3⟧’. It matches any single character in that list; if the first character of the list is the caret ‘⟦4⟧’, then it matches any character ⟦5⟧not⟦6⟧ in the list. units.sourceHTML: A bracket expression is a list of characters enclosed by ‘[’ and ‘]’. It matches any single character in that list; if the first character of the list is the caret ‘^’, then it matches any character not in the list. For example, the following command replaces the strings ‘gray’ or ‘grey’ with ‘blue’:

units.text: Bracket expressions can be used in both ⟦0⟧basic⟦1⟧ and ⟦2⟧extended⟦3⟧ regular expressions (that is, with or without the ⟦4⟧/⟦5⟧ options).
units.sourceHTML: Bracket expressions can be used in both basic and extended regular expressions (that is, with or without the -E/-r options).

units.text: Within a bracket expression, a ⟦0⟧range expression⟦1⟧ consists of two characters separated by a hyphen. It matches any single character that sorts between the two characters, inclusive. In the default C locale, the sorting sequence is the native character order; for example, ‘⟦2⟧’ is equivalent to ‘⟦3⟧’.
units.sourceHTML: Within a bracket expression, a range expression consists of two characters separated by a hyphen. It matches any single character that sorts between the two characters, inclusive. In the default C locale, the sorting sequence is the native character order; for example, ‘[a-d]’ is equivalent to ‘[abcd]’.

units.text: The characters ⟦0⟧, ⟦1⟧, ⟦2⟧, ⟦3⟧, and ⟦4⟧ are normally not special within ⟦5⟧. For example, ⟦6⟧ matches either ‘⟦7⟧’ or ‘⟦8⟧’, because the ⟦9⟧ is not special here. However, strings like ⟦10⟧, ⟦11⟧, and ⟦12⟧ are special within ⟦13⟧ and represent collating symbols, equivalence classes, and character classes, respectively, and ⟦14⟧ is therefore special within ⟦15⟧ when it is followed by ⟦16⟧, ⟦17⟧, or ⟦18⟧. Also, when not in ⟦19⟧ mode, special escapes like ⟦20⟧ and ⟦21⟧ are recognized within ⟦22⟧. See ⟦23⟧Escape Sequences - specifying special characters⟦24⟧.
units.sourceHTML: The characters $, *, ., [, and \ are normally not special within list. For example, [\*] matches either ‘\’ or ‘*’, because the \ is not special here. However, strings like [.ch.], [=a=], and [:space:] are special within list and represent collating symbols, equivalence classes, and character classes, respectively, and [ is therefore special within list when it is followed by ., =, or :. Also, when not in POSIXLY_CORRECT mode, special escapes like \n and \t are recognized within list. See Escape Sequences - specifying special characters.
